answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
When it comes to long-lived assets, like e.g. power generators or electricity infrastructure, which operate for many years or decades, purchase and investment decisions lock in path- dependencies for many years and even decades (unless these assets are prematurely retired e.g. due to economic or regulatory forcing). It is important to make such decisions based on a forward-looking assessment of the enabled average lifetime impact compared to a fair counterfactual scenario (e.g. “not making the purchase at all” or “purchasing a fossil fuel asset instead”). People often underestimate the full cumulative negative GHG emissions lifetime impact of setting up a new gas-fired powerplant that is likely to operate for the next 20-30 years. Likewise, the positive GHG emission avoidance impact enabled by setting up a new wind power plant that is likely to operate for the next 20-30 years is underestimated, too. Consequential lifetime estimates initially require working with assumptions about average performance and preliminary scenarios about how the power mix/grid intensity is expected to develop over this timeframe. After the asset has been installed and is operated by the new owner, actual data about annual yield, uptime, power mix etc allow for updating the initial assumptions by actual data.
There is a trade-off between pragmatism and accuracy. Depending on the use case, the level of precision and certainty required varies, too. A rough 80/20 internal estimate is often good enough to provide directional guidance for business decision making. In this case, demanding the resource investment for a 99% accuracy level would simply be economically unfeasible and overengineered. It would discourage making pragmatically and reasonably informed decisions. For internal business decision making, strong additionality doesn’t need to be proven, double counting is less of an issue. Indeed, it is only when actual carbon credits are issued and paid for by customers that additionality represents an important requirement and overlap (i.e. two customers paying for the same real-world impact claim) should not be allowed.
It is crucial to recognize that lifetime avoidance is enabled by multiple value chain actors in a collective impact effort, where each agent – suppliers, OEMs, planners and installers, owners and operators (and waste managers at end of life) - contributes to the outcome with different levels of quality, which can range from trivial/commodity (e.g. for standard screws, cosmetics, or standard material, which can be easily sourced and serves many industries) to substantial and fundamental (e.g. for highly specialized climate solution-related materials – e.g. SiC semiconductors - or components and services, without which the total system couldn’t function or would perform significantly worse):
1) On the supply side, up until the final handover of the installed turnkey system to the end-customer, lifetime GHG emission avoidance (estimates based on average future performance assumptions) is enabled by the upstream value chain (from raw material sourcing to planning, EPC, assembly, deliverable and installation, training). Similarly to scope 3, where overlap is a feature, not a bug, enabled avoidance (which are based on comparisons of LCAs, including scope 3) builds on another and overlaps rather than - misleadingly - adding up to 100%.
2) On the demand side, after the transfer of ownership, the potential of enabled lifetime GHG emission avoidance becomes actually realized over time (based on empirically measurable performance) by the owner and operator. Here, maintenance activities enable annual impact realization.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
The Scope 2 TWG subgroup formula is good for a very specific, limited and laborious use case: estimating scope 2 for a given year with unprecedented (and usually unnecessary) precision. But when presented as a general formula, it can be unintentionally misleading and impractical. If it is easily possible e.g. with a smart meter, accurately measuring and aggregating the *hourly* impact of electricity consumed for a single year might be most accurate for an already existing, operating asset (or purchase agreement), but seems to create unjustified workload for little impact value. In any case, when compared against the GHG intensity of electricity that would have been otherwise consumed, the scope 2 measurement represents an impact measured on the demand side, but this has little to do with broader guidance needed for consequential GHG accounting at the technology or production asset level e.g. to inform investment and business decisions.

There are many important use cases for consequential GHG accounting on the investment and supply side, e.g. when the asset in question is operating or when it is still within the value chain in the process of being delivered or has just been sold (perspective of the selling company), that don’t benefit from aggregating 8700 hourly states. Estimating the enabled impact of clean electricity production/transmission&distribution/saving/trading/consumption (for electrification purposes!) is much broader than what the scope 2 TWG subgroup formula represnets: Trying to estimate the impact of a newly installed solar PV farm or wind power farm in terms of the amount of clean electricity that is likely to *produce* during its operational lifetime (ready for transmission and distribution to the places of consumption) in order to displace a dynamic, declining average power mix (unless more specifici information is available) that would have been consumed otherwise. In this case, forward-looking annual lifetime averages serve their purpose, they are “good enough”, inspite of uncertainty, which needs to be tolerated (e.g. within a reasonable tolerance band or with conservative assumptions).

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text: Upstream GHG emissions (in gCO2e/kWh) are usually not negligible, and especially high (+15-20%) for fossil fuel -based electricity as the GHG emissions from the continuous extraction, processing, transport, including methane leakage!, need to be accounted for. Clean energy generators only incur GHG emissions once during the production process, wheras the operation and maintance is near emission-free. When distributed across average lifetime output, windpower carbon intensity including upstream GHG emissions would be within a range of e.g. ~8-15 gCO2/kWh.

answers.label: Why secondary effects should be excluded
answers.text: It is important to be consistent and transparent - when adding upstream GHG emissions for renewable energy, it should be added for fossil fuel generators or the power mix, too.

answers.label: Annual versus lifetime impact reporting
selections: Reported once for the lifetime of the project

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: Both. Both reports are not mutually exclusive. The forward-looking lifetime estimation is based on typical, average performance assumptions, the annual reporting is based on actual performance and updates the initial assumptions.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
We need to be careful about what kind of additionality is really needed and how high the burden of proof is for a given use case, and whether a proof of additionality is needed or effective at all. IF public funding or performance-linked payments, or purchases for carbon credits are involved, the burden of proof for strong/deep additionality is high, of course. This usually requires proving that e.g. for economic feasibility reasons, the project would not have been funded by a commercial investor or company (were it not for an enabling (catalytic) grant or subsidy (additionality of funding/investor impact). More generally, it may require proving that without a specific activity a specific impact could not have been possible (additionality of company/product/service impact). In case of green marketing, there is a need to make sure that impact claims are well substantiated and trustworthy, but the additionality evidence required depends on the strength of the marketing claim being made. Evidence for additionality may not be needed at all when the assessment serves internal decision making purposes. Of course the quality of an impact is higher, but in a competitive market environment, the scalability of climate solution impacts is higher when no economic concessions are needed in the first place (institutional investors are constrained by fiduciary duties and company managers are constrained by director duties). So, all tests should be optional, depending on the need for evidence and the strength of any “additionality claims” being made.

With regard to the regulatory test, the establishment of a strong mandatory regulatory standard does not suddenly nullify avoidance impacts that are enabled by companies in the value chain. If there were, for example, a sales ban of ICE cars in 2035, it would be unreasonable to conclude that from 2034 to 2035 the very real and important GHG avoidance impact of EVs would suddenly disappear or become void. Selling EVs until the last ICE has been retired is a crucial activity that must be continued regardless of supporting legislation. Company activities are crucial to make sure that the impact potential enabled by a new regulation can actually be realized. The quality of regulation matters, too. A weak regulation that legally requires what is already economic market standard has no accelerating effect on the energy transition. A strong regulation forces market share shifts to happen faster than would otherwise be observable. However, overly ambitious regulation that exceeds economic/technological capabilities of companies will again fail to make any difference in transition dynamics.

answers.text: See 27: "We need to be careful about what kind of additionality is really needed and how high the burden of proof is for a given use case, and whether a proof of additionality is needed or effective at all..."

answers.label: Additionality tests missing from the framework
answers.text: When the goal is to prove that a renewable energy project would not have been fundable without a subsidy, an assessment of economic feasibility (e.g. a "marginal carbon abatement cost curve"!) should be not too difficult to conduct. Feedback from mainstream investors who confirm that the WACC is too high for their mandate, or the risk-return-profile is not good fit with their mandate, would also constitute strong evidence.

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text: It depends on the context. It is well known that in emerging economics risk perceptions and capital costs – as well as operational asset performance conditions – can vary, often capital costs are higher in developed economies, to some extent due to perceptions (prejudices) about country and currency risks that are not aligned with economic reality. The fact that subsidies or grant funding is needed for a rapid transition is a sign of market failure (to price in positive and negative externalities, and regulatory failure to do so) that applies not only to emerging but also developed market economies. In addition, developing economies suffer from greater capital market inefficiencies.

answers.label: Claims possible under different test approaches
answers.text: Of course. Please keep in mind that avoidance-based carbon credits are one of few commercialized impact claims where additionality is paid for by customers who would not want to double-play. The same applies to public grant funding. But except for these niche use cases, an additionality claim - and the rigor it requires when done right - is NOT something that anyone wants or even should pay for. Companies active within a climate solution value chain do not need to make “exclusive” causality claims, they can articulate a claim so that it acknowledges the collective impact effort and the importance of the contribution of other agents. A good way to do so is to communicate “enabled” impact (where the same impact can be enabled by multiple parties at once) rather than monocausally “caused” impact. Moreover, climate solution companies should not create the impression as if enabled lifetime avoidance was “real” or that it has already been realized at the time climate solution value chain products and services are sold and delivered. They can communicate that the enabled impact potential still needs to be realized by the end-customers, owners and operators over time.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text: UNLESS 1) you are a research institute or think tank with a mandate and ample resources to provide policy advice based on a comprehensive simulation of the entire transnational grid system, OR 2) the impact is based on a specific charge and discharge pattern (battery storage, demand flexibility) these methods are overengineered, exclusive, impractical. For most business and investment decisions analysts will simply want to use the annual average grid emission factors that are easily publicy accessible e.g. via Our World in Data (for production) or Nowtricty (for consumption) to estimate a reasonable empirical baseline / counterfactual scenario for a given year.

answers.label: Assessing model applicability to project types
answers.text: Real-world-based energy system modeling in order to inform policy and public investment decisions is an engineering discipline. What does this have to do with the GHG Protocol and the vast majority of its users? In general, I don't think it would be fair to diminish the positive GHG avoidance impact potential of clean energy generators and electrification due to past government's planning and public investment shortcomings that lead to an inefficient power grid and failure to expand the grid as much as would have been needed in time. The installer of a new wind power generator, who has no influence on the grid, it should be reasonable to assume a functional T&D system and for the grid operator, it should be an urgent priority to ensure this.

answers.label: Other appropriate emission rates or metrics
answers.text:
Note that it is the installed base that is causing annual GHG emissions. If its composition changes, average GHG intensity changes.
It is only when a low intensity technology has fully replaced the incumbent high intensity technology that the optimal intensity level is reached
Constant efficiency improvments are also important to ensure that the emissions intensity of a modernizing installed base continuously declines
Some use cases:
- Efficiency improvements enable electricity savings which enable 1) avoiding average grid consumption and/or 2) consumption and electrification elsewhere within the system
- Clean electricity enables clean electrification
- Grid expansion, replacement, repair enables electrification

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: How can this be specified as a general standard? Depends on the use case, the context, the climate solution technology, the goal, the available resources, the accessible data etc. Even the country level is not the maximum appropriate level. If a company doesn't exactly know in which countries its products and services are sold and used downstream, regional or global average emission factors may serve as the next best preliminary proxies until better becomes available. Moreover, we don't want to discourage expansion of renewable electricity or electricity saving in countries which have already a near optimal clean electricity grid - they need it to enable avoidance through electrification, and - most importantly- in a transnational grid system where electricity is traded, they can and should export excess clean energy to other grid-connected countries.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: Again, how can this be specified as a general standard? Depends on the use case, the context, the climate solution technology, the goal, the available resources, the accessible data etc. Barries and smart meters require higher granularity. Rough lifetime estimates may work with annual averages and a range of scenarios that anticipate developments in mix and demand for decades ahead, which ultimately depends on past as well as future policy and public investment decisions. Let’s keep in mind: Only because something cannot be measured (i.e. needs to be roughly estimated) doesn’t mean that it cannot or shouldn’t be effectively managed (with foresight).

answers.text: This is dependent on factors that a project cannot influence and change over time during the course of the project. Policies, rules and incentives change all the time. The grid system needs to meet the need of a Paris aligned economy, with, increased demand, increased volatility and increased levels of electrification. To this en,d the grid needs to be interregionally intergrated, and it needs to utilize sufficient battery and long duration storage alongside demand response solutions and flexible fossil peakers, but only as a last resort, and at a minimum leves, which is entirely feasible with sufficient political will, planning and investment.
